lesson.title: 1492: Columbus, the Bahamas, and a World Forever Changed
lesson.summary: This section covers Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage across the Atlantic, his mistaken belief that he had reached Asia, and the beginning of sustained contact between Europe and the Americas, along with the violence that followed.
lesson.body:
Christopher Columbus was born around 1451 in Genoa, in what is now Italy, and spent years trying to persuade European monarchs to fund a westward voyage across the Atlantic Ocean, which he believed would provide a shorter route to Asia than the route Portugal was pursuing around Africa. Most educated Europeans of the time actually had a reasonably accurate sense of the Earth's circumference and correctly judged that Columbus had badly underestimated the distance involved, but in 1492, fresh off the completion of the Reconquista discussed earlier in this unit, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain agreed to finance the voyage, hoping for a share in whatever wealth it might bring.

Columbus departed the Spanish port of Palos de la Frontera on August 3, 1492, commanding three ships, the Nina, the Pinta, and the Santa Maria. After more than two months at sea, land was sighted on October 12, 1492, an island in the Bahamas that Columbus named San Salvador. He had not reached Asia. He had reached the Caribbean, home to the Taino people and other indigenous societies who had lived there for many centuries, part of the broader world of pre-Columbian civilizations discussed earlier in this unit. Columbus, convinced he had arrived near the East Indies, called the people he met Indians, a mistaken label that nonetheless stuck and was applied for centuries afterward to the many distinct indigenous peoples of the Americas.

It is worth being precise about what Columbus's voyage was, and was not. He was not the first person to reach the Americas, since millions of indigenous people already lived there, nor was he even the first European, since Norse voyagers under Leif Erikson had reached the coast of Newfoundland roughly five centuries earlier, around the year 1000, establishing a short lived settlement whose remains have been confirmed by archaeologists at a site called L'Anse aux Meadows. What made 1492 different, and historically decisive, was that Columbus's voyage initiated sustained, continuous contact between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres, setting off the enormous exchange of people, goods, and diseases explored later in this unit.

Columbus made three more voyages to the Caribbean and the coasts of Central and South America between 1493 and 1504, but his time as a colonial administrator was marked by mismanagement, violence toward indigenous peoples, and harsh forced labor systems imposed on the Taino population of Hispaniola, the island now divided between Haiti and the Dominican Republic. Columbus demanded tribute in gold and imposed brutal punishments on those who failed to deliver it, contributing to a rapid and severe decline in the Taino population. His conduct as governor became notorious enough that in 1500 Spanish authorities arrested him and sent him back to Spain in chains, though he was later released.

Columbus died in Spain in 1506, still believing he had reached the outskirts of Asia. His voyages opened the door to Spanish conquest of the Americas, explored in the next section through the conquistadors who followed him, and set in motion changes, biological, economic, and political, that would permanently transform both sides of the Atlantic world.
